{{DISPLAYTITLE:Induction, as the machine sees it}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Inductive types and recursors|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Structural and well-founded recursion}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Proof by induction is the standard way to prove something about every natural number. In
Lean it is not a separate rule added to the logic. It is the recursion principle of
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Building things from constructors|building things from
constructors]], put to work on proofs. This page shows the two cases, the tactic that sets
them up, and what Lean records once the proof is finished.

== The familiar form ==

To prove that a statement holds for every natural number, two things are enough. First,
prove it for 0: the '''base case'''. Second, prove that whenever it holds for a number k, it
also holds for k + 1: the '''induction step''', in which "it holds for k" is the
'''induction hypothesis'''. Then the statement holds for 0, so for 1, so for 2, and so on,
with no number left out.

== Why it is the recursion principle ==

The natural numbers in Lean are made by two rules: zero, and the successor of a number
already made. From those rules Lean derives a recursion principle: to produce something for
every number, give it for zero, and give a way to go from what it is for n to what it is for
n + 1. Now let the thing produced be a proof of the statement about n. The principle then
says: given a proof for zero, and a way to turn a proof for k into a proof for k + 1, there
is a proof for every number. That is induction, word for word. Theorem Proving in Lean 4
describes the induction principle as just a special case of the recursion principle, the
case in which what is produced is a proof.<ref name="tpil-ind">Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de
Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich, ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'' (online edition for
Lean 4.33.0, lean-lang.org), chapter 7, "Inductive Types".
https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Inductive-Types/</ref>

Induction is therefore not an extra axiom. It comes with the type of natural numbers,
derived from its two constructors, and the same holds for every type defined by
constructors.<ref name="ref-ind">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0
(lean-lang.org, 2026), section 4.4, "Inductive Types".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/</ref>

== Two equations that look alike ==

Addition in Lean is defined by recursion on the second number: n + 0 is n, and n + (m + 1)
is (n + m) + 1.<ref name="tpil-ind" /> That makes one equation true by computation alone.
<code>rfl</code> is the proof that says "both sides compute to the same thing", and Lean
accepts it here:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example (n : Nat) : n + 0 = n := rfl
</pre>

The mirror image is refused:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n := by rfl
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 replies <code>Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side</code>, then that
<code>0 + n</code> "is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side" <code>n</code>. The
reason is plain once the definition is in view. To compute 0 + n, Lean must know whether n
is zero or a successor, and n is unknown. Both statements are true; only the first is true
by computation. The second needs induction.<ref name="tpil-ind" />

== The induction tactic ==

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem zero_add' (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k ih => rw [Nat.add_succ, ih]

#print zero_add'
</pre>

The line <code>induction n</code> replaces one task by two, one for each way a natural number
can be made, and adds an induction hypothesis wherever a constructor takes a number of the
same type.<ref name="ref-tacref">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0
(lean-lang.org, 2026), section 14.5, "Tactic Reference": entries for <code>induction</code>
and <code>rw</code>. https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/</ref>
Inside the two cases, Lean's display of what remains to be proved reads:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
case zero
⊢ 0 + 0 = 0

case succ
k : Nat
ih : 0 + k = k
⊢ 0 + (k + 1) = k + 1
</pre>

The symbol ⊢ marks what must be shown; the lines above it are what may be used. The base
case, 0 + 0 = 0, holds by computation, and <code>rfl</code> closes it. In the step, Lean has
named the number <code>k</code> and the induction hypothesis <code>ih</code>. The tactic
<code>rw</code> rewrites the goal with an equation. First it uses <code>Nat.add_succ</code>,
the fact that n + (m + 1) equals (n + m) + 1, which turns the goal into (0 + k) + 1 = k + 1.
Then it uses <code>ih</code> to replace 0 + k by k. The two sides now agree, and
<code>rw</code> closes the goal by itself.<ref name="ref-tacref" /> How goals are displayed
and filled is the subject of [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Holes and goals|holes and
goals]].

== What Lean records ==

The <code>#print</code> line shows the proof that Lean actually kept:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem zero_add' : ∀ (n : Nat), 0 + n = n :=
fun n =>
  Nat.recAux (Eq.refl (0 + 0))
    (fun k ih =>
      Eq.mpr (id (congrArg (fun _a => _a = k + 1) (Nat.add_succ 0 k)))
        (Eq.mpr (id (congrArg (fun _a => _a.succ = k + 1) ih)) (Eq.refl k.succ)))
    n
</pre>

The tactic script is gone. In its place is a single expression, and at its head stands
<code>Nat.recAux</code>. Asked to print that name, Lean shows that it is
<code>Nat.rec</code>, the recursion principle itself, written with 0 and n + 1 in place of
the constructor names. Its first argument, <code>Eq.refl (0 + 0)</code>, is the base case:
0 + 0 computes to 0, so the equation is an instance of a thing being equal to itself. Its second, <code>fun k ih =&gt;
...</code>, is the step: a function that takes a number k and a proof for k and returns a
proof for k + 1. The rest of the step records the two rewrites. This expression, and not the
script, is what the Lean kernel checks.

== A formula from school ==

The sum 1 + 2 + ... + n is half of n(n + 1). In whole numbers it is cleaner to say that twice
the sum is n(n + 1):

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def sumTo : Nat → Nat
  | 0     => 0
  | n + 1 => (n + 1) + sumTo n

#eval sumTo 100

theorem two_mul_sumTo (n : Nat) : 2 * sumTo n = n * (n + 1) := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k ih =>
    simp only [sumTo, Nat.mul_add, Nat.add_mul] at *
    omega
</pre>

The <code>#eval</code> line prints <code>5050</code>, which is half of 100 × 101. The proof has the same two cases. The base case holds by computation. In the step,
<code>simp only</code> unfolds <code>sumTo</code> once and multiplies out the brackets, in
the goal and in the induction hypothesis alike, and <code>omega</code>, an arithmetic
procedure described in [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Automation and its limits|automation
and its limits]], finishes the sum.

== Other types, other inductions ==

Every type defined by constructors has its own recursor, so every such type has its own
induction. For lists: prove the statement for the empty list, then prove it for a list with
an item in front, assuming it for the rest. For the trees of
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Building things from constructors|building things from
constructors]]: prove it for a leaf, then for a node, assuming it for both subtrees, since
the recursor for trees supplies a hypothesis for each. The <code>induction</code> tactic
works the same way for all of them.<ref name="ref-tacref" />
